deep.reconstruction:
Context (from §§546–550 on the previous page): Euler wants to prove the converse of the product formula. If a²+b² divides p²+q², is the quotient also a sum of two squares? He then uses this to prove Fermat's theorem that every prime of the form 4n+1 is a sum of two squares.

Setup of §550. Take a, b coprime. Write p = m a − n b and q = n a + m b + s. Since (ma−nb)² + (na+mb)² = (a²+b²)(m²+n²), we get
p² + q² = (a²+b²)(m²+n²) + s(s + 2(na+mb)).

§551. If P = a²+b² is prime and divides p²+q², then P divides s(s+2(na+mb)). Hence P divides one of the two factors.
- Case 1: s = tP. Then (p²+q²)/P = m²+n² + t(tP + 2(na+mb)). Expanding gives m² + 2mbt + t²b² + n² + 2nat + a²t² = (m+bt)² + (n+at)².

§552. Case 2: s + 2(na+mb) = tP, so s = tP − 2(na+mb). Then s(s+2(na+mb)) = s·tP, and the quotient is m²+n² + t²P − 2t(na+mb) = (m−bt)² + (n−at)².
- So in both cases the quotient of a sum of two squares by a prime sum of two squares is again a sum of two squares.

§553. Contrapositive: if the quotient is not a sum of two squares, the divisor is not a prime of the form a²+b². Divisor and quotient may be interchanged.

§554. Let A, B, C be primes that are sums of two squares. Apply §551–552 repeatedly: (p²+q²)/A = r²+s², then (r²+s²)/B = t²+u², then (t²+u²)/C = x²+y². Hence (p²+q²)/(ABC) = x²+y².

§§555–556. Suppose p²+q² has a divisor N that is not a sum of two squares. By §554 with the roles of divisor and quotient swapped, the cofactor cannot be a product of primes that are sums of two squares. So among the remaining prime factors at least one is not a sum of two squares.

§§557–560: Fermat–Euler descent.
- Assume a sum of two coprime squares p²+q² is divisible by some 𝔄 that is not a sum of two squares.
- Since (p−m𝔄)² + (q−n𝔄)² ≡ p²+q² (mod 𝔄), reduce p and q to absolute residues |p|, |q| ≤ 𝔄/2. Using 𝔄−p if necessary, as in §558.
- Then p²+q² < 𝔄²/2, so the quotient 𝔅 = (p²+q²)/𝔄 satisfies 𝔅 < 𝔄/2.
- By §556, 𝔅 either is itself not a sum of two squares or has such a factor.
- Repeat with 𝔅: get r²+s² < 𝔅²/2, with quotient ℭ < 𝔅/2, again a non-sum. Then 𝔇 < ℭ/2, and so on.
- §561 (next page) concludes by infinite descent that this is absurd. §562 adds that −1 is a quadratic residue of a prime 4n+1, which gives Fermat's two-square theorem.

The marginal note (*) asserts that the reduced roots remain coprime if p and q are.
errors: Marginal note (*) is false as stated. Take p=17, q=6 (coprime) and 𝔄=13: 17²+6² = 325 = 13·25. The half-reduced roots are (4,6), with gcd 2 (16+36 = 52 = 13·4). What is true and needed is weaker: any common factor d of the reduced roots is coprime to 𝔄 (a common prime of d and 𝔄 would divide both p and q). So d can be divided out without destroying divisibility by 𝔄. The gap is easily repaired but is not addressed on this page.

Coprimality is essential and is used only implicitly: it guarantees the reduced residues are not both 0 mod 𝔄, so the descent does not collapse to 0 (e.g. 3²+3² is divisible by 3). In §560 Euler silently assumes coprimality persists at each step; see the previous item.
§558–559: the bound should be p, q ≤ 𝔄/2 rather than strictly less (when 𝔄 is even, the residue 𝔄/2 is possible). This gives 𝔅 ≤ 𝔄/2, which still suffices for descent.

§560 is loose: it calls the quotient ℭ itself 'not a sum of two squares'. Strictly, by §556 one should pass to a factor of 𝔅 (or of the new quotient) that is not a sum of two squares. That factor is ≤ the quotient, so the descent is unaffected.
§551–552 tacitly need P = a²+b² prime, so that P | s(s+2(na+mb)) forces P | s or P | s+2(na+mb). Euler states this restriction in §549, so this is correct as used.

results.what: If a prime P = a²+b² divides p²+q², then (p²+q²)/P is a sum of two squares. Proof via p = ma−nb, q = na+mb+s, splitting into two cases.
results.modern_name: Lemma: quotient of a sum of two squares by a prime sum of two squares (norm divisibility in Z[i])
results.usually_credited_to: Euler (letters to Goldbach 1747–49; E228, E241, published 1758/1760)

results.what: Iteration to products of primes of the form a²+b² (§554), and the contrapositive that a non-sum divisor forces a non-sum prime factor in the cofactor (§§555–556).
results.modern_name: Multiplicativity / closure of norms from Z[i]

results.what: Descent: reduce p, q mod 𝔄 to |p|, |q| ≤ 𝔄/2, giving a quotient below 𝔄/2 that is again (or has a factor) not a sum of two squares; infinite descent gives a contradiction. Divisors of a sum of two coprime squares are sums of two squares.
results.modern_name: Euler's infinite-descent proof of Fermat's two-square theorem (divisor lemma)

deep.surprise_reason: This is the Tractatus de numerorum doctrina (E792, published posthumously 1849) and reproduces Euler's well-known descent proof of the two-squares theorem from E241/E228 and his Goldbach letters. The only small points of interest are the false marginal remark on coprimality and the case-split form of the prime-divisor lemma; both are minor.

checkable.asserts: Shifting p, q by multiples of 𝔄 preserves divisibility by 𝔄 (§557).
Counterexample to the marginal note: reduced roots (4,6) of coprime (17,6) are not coprime.

checkable.sympy: all(any(x**2+y**2==P for x in range(P) for y in range(P)) for P in primerange(2,500) if P%4==1)
checkable.asserts: Primes 4n+1 below 500 are sums of two squares (the conclusion the descent serves).

transcription_corrections: Transcription matches the image in all substantive respects; the only discrepancy is a stray mark before 'poterit' in §560 ("exhiberi 'poterit") on the page, which is not a textual difference.
Fraktur letters 𝔄, 𝔅, ℭ, 𝔇 are correctly rendered as \mathfrak{A}, ..., \mathfrak{D}.
